@agntn/web: # @agntn/web npm version npm downloads license Ask DeepWiki 🔎 Thirteen search APIs, one `{ url, title, snippet }`. You ask Exa, Brave or your own SearXNG the same way, you read the page behind a hit the same way, and nobody has to remember whose key goes in which header. ## Why? Every search API sells the same thing, ten links with a title and a snippet, and every one of them takes the order differently. Exa wants a POST with `x-api-key`, Brave a GET with `X-Subscription-Token`, Tavily puts the key inside the JSON body, why not. Wire three of those into an agent and you have three clients, three response shapes and three ideas of what a date looks like. So this is one class shape in front of thirteen of them, search, read and reverse image search, same objects out no matter who answered.

@ksankar/pi-monitor: # pi-monitor Wake the agent once when a background command finishes, matches output, or goes quiet. So any edit that overlaps text changed by an earlier edit — a very natural thing for a model to write — is rejected after the first edit has already succeeded. - **The retry loop is expensive.** The model re-reads the file, re-derives all the edits, and tries again. anti-gpt-slop: # anti-gpt-slop **Make Luna Great Again.** 🌕 English | 中文 一个 Pi 扩展：在 GPT 的回答交付给用户之前，用内置规则审一遍，发现它在装模作样、甩锅、自我辩护而不是真的在干活，就打回去让它重写。 ## 起源：一篇叫《应试智能》的锐评 这个插件的规则集不是凭空定的风格偏好，是直接照着一篇流传的《应试智能》锐评文章里列的 GPT 症状写的。那篇文章的核心判断是：GPT 的每一个回答都像是写给一个想象中的阅卷老师——多写不扣分，说错才扣分，于是它宁可又臭又长又绕、句句加限定，也不肯说一句可能被追责的话。字面要求全部完成，真正想要的东西一样没懂。 文章拆出来的几种典型症状，直接对应到这个插件的规则里： **逃避责任 / 防御性写作** —— 原文点名的口癖是"这不代表 XXX""不能说明 XXX"，装进代码里就是"过度编程"，过小溪造航母，还在航母上写免责声明。这对应规则里 Section 0 的 Zero Conversational Wrapper 和 Section 4 禁止的"这不代表……""不能说明……""不等于……"。 **习惯性否定 / 稻草人式"不是而是"** —— 文章总结的规律是："不是而是"前半句否定的内容，至少三分之二是用户根本不会有的误解"；还有把问题偷换成更好回答的版本（"真正要回答的不是 XXX，而是 XXX"）。这正是规则 Section 4 禁止的"不是……而是……""真正要考虑的不是 X，而是 Y"。 **黑话和语癖** —— 文章原样列出的一串词："稳稳接住、不躲不藏不绕、先给结论、补一刀、收口、骨架、根因、落盘、口径、终态、底牌、压实、收束、链路、兜底、闭环、拉通、抓手"。这份清单几乎原样搬进了规则 Section 4 的 Banned Jargon & Verbal Tics。

pi-context-tax: # pi-context-tax Part of how I work is shipping slop and then converging. I try things, see what sticks, and clean up as I go. My coding environment goes through the same cycle: I try new skills, plugins, and MCPs, and end up keeping things around that I don't need in the long term. That comes with a startup tax. pi-next-turn: # pi-next-turn Predicts your next prompt in pi, and, if you let it, works on it before you send it. After each run, pi-next-turn asks forks of your session what you will type next. The forks reuse your session's prompt cache, so a prediction costs mostly cache reads. A confident prediction is shown below the editor (and on your phone with pi-mobile). That is all it does by default. Working ahead is opt-in, at two levels: - `/next-turn ahead read`: above a higher bar it also reads the files that prompt will need while you are still reading. Read-only. - `/next-turn ahead draft`: it also runs the whole predicted turn ahead of time and holds its edits in an in-memory pi-multiedit draft. Send that prompt and the prepared turn appears at once, its edits applied all-or-nothing. Send anything els

One follows a failed edit, the other follows a successful one. ## After a failed edit When pi's own edit cannot find the old text, or finds it more than once, it reports the miss and nothing else. The retry usually starts with a re-read, and often misses again because the old text was written from memory. The hint appends the closest region as it reads on disk now, with line numbers and current text, so the retry copies real lines. Matching is by line agreement, not character similarity. It watches the model's streamed thinking and its finished runs, and when the same work keeps coming back, it cuts the response off and tells the model to change its approach. It catches loops inside a single thought as it streams, including the two ways streaming models collapse in practice: a phrase or single token repeated forever (such as `= the = the = the`), and reasoning that falls apart into runs of punctuation (such as `= = = =`).
